newsitem.title: UK: UK War Crimes Act controversial from start.
newsitem.headline: UK War Crimes Act controversial from start.

text.p: The 1991 War Crimes Act under which Szymon Serafinowicz was charged with murdering three Jews during World War Two, was one of the most controversial laws Britain ever passed.
The government had to invoke a special power, not previously used for 40 years, to force it through parliament after it was thrown out by the upper house of parliament, the House of Lords.
The law allows Britain to prosecute suspected war criminals even though their crimes were committed on foreign soil.

On Friday, a jury at London's Old Bailey decided that Serafinowicz was mentally unfit to stand trial, casting serious doubt over whether an alleged war criminal will ever be brought to trial in Britain.

The House of Lords, which includes a large number of elderly peers who lived through the war, voted down the bill, arguing that it was unreasonable to try someone for a crime that happened half a century ago.
One of its most vocal opponents was Lord Shawcross, Britain's chief prosecutor at the Nuremburg trials.
Serafinowicz was the first person to be charged under the act although a special police unit set up after the act to uncover suspected war criminals had looked into 350 cases.
Most of those suspects have now either died or been cleared and the unit is believed to be investigating only about half a dozen cases.

Serafinowicz's case is believed to have been the one the unit thought most likely to succeed in court, although Britain's Crown Prosecution Service (CPS) said it still has five cases that it is considering taking to trial.
"What happens in this case won't influence the others. Each will be judged on its own merits," said a CPS spokeswoman.

The nearest Britain had previously come to holding a warcrimes trial was in 1994 when a retired Lithuanian mining engineer, Anton Gecas, sued for libel after a television report accused him of killing Jews during World War Two.
Gecas lost his case when the judge ruled that he was satisfied he was a mass murderer, but said there was not enough evidence to try him for war crimes.
Trials of war crimes dating from World War Two have proved equally fraught with difficulty in other countries.

The case of Erich Priebke provoked outrage in Italy last year when a court found the former SS captain guilty of the massacre of 335 men and boys in 1944, but said he was no longer liable for punishment.
The verdict was later overturned and a new trial ordered, but Italy is still wrangling over which court should try him.

In 1993, Israel's supreme court overturned the conviction of John Demjanjuk, a retired U.S. autoworker wrongly accused of being "Ivan the Terrible", a notorious guard who ran the gas chamber at the Nazi death camp Treblinka.
Demjanjuk, only the second alleged Nazi war criminal to be tried by Israel, had been convicted on the basis of identification by eye-witnesses.
Although the court established that he had been a guard in other death camps in Poland and Germany, Demjanjuk was freed.
Prosecutions in Australia and Canada have also failed at a cost of millions of dollars.
In France, "the butcher of Lyons," Klaus Barbie, was found guilty of murder in absentia after fleeing the country.
By the time he returned to France his conviction was no longer valid so he was retried and sentenced in 1987 for crimes against humanity. He died in prison four years later.
A French court is currently deciding whether or not to try former cabinet minister Maurice Papon for crimes against humanity allegedly committed during World War Two.
